title: Living in Argentina | The Country That Has Been Losing Its Money for 100 Years — but Never Its Joy
fullText: [music] >> There is a land where waterfalls thunder along a cliff wider than entire towns, >> [music] >> where mountains wear a dozen colors at once, where walls of ancient ice crack like cannon fire and crash into the lakes below. This is Argentina. >> [music] >> And yet the greatest wonder anyone has ever [music] seen here was not made of water, rock, or ice. It appeared on one summer night in the capital, a single crowd of millions singing and weeping around a white [music] obelisk. Not for a revolution, not for the end of a war, for a football match. >> [music] [music] >> So stay for the whole journey, from the thundering falls to the quietest cafe in Buenos Aires, and you will understand what few [music] outsiders ever do. Why this country, of all places, [music] needs football more than anywhere else on Earth, and why on any ordinary Sunday afternoon its loudest city still falls [music] suddenly perfectly silent. Begin with breakfast, which in Buenos Aires is a small act of resistance against the modern world. A coffee, a media luna, the local croissant, >> [music] >> smaller, denser, and sweeter, and above all time. In this city, you can sit in a cafe for 2 hours over a single cup, and nobody will bring the bill, because bringing the bill uninvited would be rude. You ask for it when you are ready. Some mornings, nobody is [music] ever quite ready. The city takes its cafes so seriously that it protects them by law. More than 70 are officially listed as Bares Notables, notable bars, historic rooms >> [music] >> declared part of the city's cultural heritage. The oldest is Cafe Tortoni, pouring coffee [music] on the Avenida de Mayo since 1858. Tango legend Carlos Gardel drank here. So did [music] the writer Jorge Luis Borges. The marble tables and stained glass look much as they did when those regulars were alive. In Buenos Aires, a cafe is not a business. It is a room where the city keeps its memory. A short walk away stands what may be the most beautiful bookshop on the planet, and that is not a slogan. El Ateneo Grand Splendid opened in 1919 as a theater, all balconies, painted dome, and crimson stage curtain. In the year 2000, [music] it became a bookstore, and almost nothing was removed. Readers browse novels in the old theater boxes, [music] and the cafe sits directly on the stage. When National Geographic went looking for the world's most beautiful bookshop in 2019, it simply handed this one the crown. >> [music] >> The city reads late, eats later, and thinks about all of it professionally. Dinner at 10:00 is normal. The theaters of Corrientes Avenue are still filling at midnight. And when it all becomes too much, when Osiris talks it through. By World [music] Health Organization counts, Argentina has more psychologists per person than any other country on Earth, several times the rate of the United States. This is a place that takes its feelings seriously. [music] Which turns out to be necessary, because to understand daily life here, you have to open a wallet and take a deep breath. For most of a century, money in Argentina has behaved like weather. Something that happens to you. Something you check [music] every morning. This was once one of the richest countries in the world. A place [music] Europe sent its hopeful to for a better life. Then came a hundred years of booms, busts, defaults, and devaluations that economists still argue about. Whoever was to blame, and every family here has an opinion, ordinary people learned one lesson deep in their bones. Paper money is a promise, >> [music] >> and promises can break. >> [music] >> You can read that lesson in [music] the small habits of daily life. Big purchases counted out in bricks of banknotes, fed through counting machines while everyone waits politely. >> [music] >> Two prices for the same item, one for cash, one for card [music] because card fees quietly eat several percent. Gym memberships that rise mid-contract, menus with new prices taped over old ones, rental [music] contracts once written just months long because nobody could guess what money would be worth [music] in six. And a national instinct to spend [music] quickly because for as long as anyone can remember, a bill saved was a bill shrinking. And then >> [music] >> there are the dollars. For decades, Argentines converted their savings into American dollars the moment they could and hid them in home safes, in deposit boxes, famously under mattresses. [music] When governments restricted buying them, a parallel street market bloomed with its own exchange [music] rate published daily and quiet men on downtown corners murmuring a single word, cambio, exchange, to everyone walking past. An entire nation [music] became fluent in a second currency it rarely touches. These last few years, the story has taken a sharp turn. A new government tore up the old currency controls [music] in 2025. The parallel exchange rates converged into one, and monthly inflation fell from crisis levels to low [music] single digits. For the first time in a generation, the storm seems to be easing. [music] And here is the most Argentine detail of all. Almost nobody fully believes it yet. The dollars stay hidden. The habits stay in the bones. >> [music] >> In a country [music] burned this many times, hope is something you keep, but never something you store your savings in. >> [music] >> So, when money [music] cannot be trusted to hold its value, people build their lives around [music] things that can. And Argentines, over one difficult century, have assembled [music] a magnificent collection of them. The first one fits in one hand. Mate is a bitter [music] green infusion drunk from a hollow gourd through a metal straw called a bombilla, and it is less a beverage than a ceremony. One person prepares it, sips first, refills it, and passes it around the circle. Everyone drinks from the same straw. You do not stir it. You do not adjust it, and you do not say thank you. Not until you mean, "I am finished." Sharing mate with a stranger is a quiet declaration [music] of trust, which is exactly the point. >> In a country trained to doubt its institutions, people built a daily ritual whose entire message is you and I are fine. The day has other fixed stars. Around 5:00 in the afternoon comes merienda, coffee and something [music] sweet. Defended by school children and grandmothers with equal seriousness. And after dinner comes [music] the most Argentine hour of all, the one English has no word for, sobremesa. [music] The meal is over, the plates are empty, and nobody moves. You stay at the table, talking, arguing, laughing, pouring one more glass, often for longer than the meal itself lasted. Leaving right after [music] eating is considered, in this country, faintly suspicious behavior. The table is not there for the food. [clears throat] The food is an excuse [music] for the table. Once a month, the calendar itself sets the menu. On the 29th, kitchens across Argentina serve gnocchis, [music] potato gnocchi carried over by Italian immigrants, and many families slide a bank note under the plate for luck and prosperity [music] in the month ahead. One origin story ties the date to an Italian saint. The other is simpler. By the 29th, the month's money was gone, and potatoes and flour were what the pantry had left. Hardship became [music] a recipe. The recipe became a ritual, and the ritual outlived the hardship. Argentines like the joke so much they named their ghost employees after it. A ñoqui is a worker who only appears on the 29th to collect a salary. [music] But the greatest ritual of them all does not happen in a kitchen. It happens on a patch of bare ground behind the houses wherever a ball can bounce. Every Argentine footballer, from the greatest to the long forgotten, points back at the same origin. The potrero. A potrero is a scrap of unused ground, a dusty lot, a dried-out field, a concrete corner between buildings. Claimed by children and converted by common consent into a stadium. No referee [music] no lines, no mercy. The ball bounces badly, the space is cramped, and the older boys do not go [music] easy. Out of exactly those conditions [music] came the tight control and the low cunning that the world calls Argentine style. The old joke here is told with [music] pride. Other countries build academies. Argentina [music] builds vacant lots. >> [cheering] >> One step up from the potrero [music] stands an institution that visitors rarely hear about, the neighborhood club. There are thousands of them across the country. Modest buildings with a court, a hall, and a grill where children learn football and chess, families hold birthday parties, and grandparents [music] play cards on Friday nights. >> [music] >> For over a century, these little clubs have been the living rooms of Argentine neighborhoods. The giants like Boca and River get the headlines. The club de barrio is where the country actually grows up. >> [music] >> 300 km up the river from the capital [music] lies Rosario, a working port city with an improbable record [music] of producing geniuses. In one modest neighborhood here, in the late 1990s, a very small boy [music] played on the local dirt with a ball that seemed tied to his left foot. Doctors diagnosed a growth hormone deficiency. The treatment cost more than his family could manage. [music] A club in Barcelona eventually agreed to pay for it, and the boy left home at 13. His name was Lionel Messi. >> [music] >> Today, his city paints him across entire [music] buildings, murals several stories tall watching over the same streets [music] where he learned everything. >> [music] >> And the greatest legend of all came from the poorest ground of all. Diego Maradona grew up in Villa Fiorito, a struggling settlement on the southern [music] edge of Buenos Aires, playing on dirt that barely qualified as a field. Argentines have never separated those two facts. The gift and the dust belong together. Proof, renewed once a generation, that a vacant lot can be hiding a miracle. But to see where all of this began, the game, the music, the whole mythology, you have to travel back down the river to a port neighborhood painted every color at once. >> [music] >> La Boca, the mouth, sits where a muddy river opens toward the sea. And for decades, it was Argentina's [music] front door. Ships unloaded here through the great immigration years, >> [music] >> when this country absorbed millions of Italians, Spaniards, [music] and others chasing a promise. The newcomers packed into conventillos, shared tenement houses, one family [music] to a room, and painted the corrugated walls with whatever half tins of paint the shipyards discarded. [music] That is why [music] the famous Caminito alley looks the way it does, blue beside yellow beside green. [music] It was never a design choice. It was leftovers >> [music] >> turned into an identity. >> [music] >> In those crowded courtyards and dockside bars, a music was born. Tango took its heartbeat from Candombe. >> [music] >> The drumming of the Afro-Argentine communities of these river ports, added the immigrants homesickness [music] and the sigh of the bandoneon and became the saddest music you can dance in an embrace. Polite society was scandalized by it >> [music] >> until Paris fell in love and Buenos Aires finally forgave its own invention. It began among people who owned almost nothing, which may be why a century later it still sounds [music] like longing. >> [music] >> A few streets away rises a stadium unlike any other on Earth. In the 1930s, the architect [music] Victor Sulčič kept bringing a birthday present to design meetings, a box of chocolates [music] whose shape looked suspiciously like the steep, strange arena his team was drawing. [music] The name stuck forever. La Bombonera, >> [music] >> the chocolate box, three vertiginous stands and one flat vertical wall squeezed into a single city block. Holding around 57,000 people [music] who all seem to land at once when they jump. On big match days, the structure visibly sways. Engineers [music] insist it is safe. The locals put it better than any engineer ever could. La Bombonera does not tremble, they [music] say, it beats. >> [applause] [music] >> In another country, that would be a stadium. [music] Here, it is a temple. And Argentina takes its temples further than anywhere else on Earth. >> [music] >> In 1998 in Rosario, three friends, among them a young man named Hernán Améz, did something halfway between a joke and a confession of faith. They founded a church for Diego Maradona. The Iglesia Maradoniana has its own commandments, its own calendar counting the years from Diego's birth, and its own Christmas celebrated [music] on the 30th of October, his birthday. Its god is written D10S, [music] the Spanish word for god, with Maradona's number 10 >> [music] >> hiding inside it. Today, it claims more than 100,000 members across the world. Ask a member whether they are serious and you receive the most Argentine answer available, completely, and also not at all. Even those who worship nothing keep the [music] rituals. During big tournaments, the whole country runs on cabalas, private superstitions handled with the gravity of law. The lucky shirt that must not be washed while the team keeps winning. The beard that must not be shaved. The exact [music] seat on the exact couch beside the exact same people [music] as the last victory, reassembled for every match like evidence in a trial. [music] Grandmothers time their prayers to kick off. Nobody here calls any of this irrational because within [music] living memory it has worked three times. >> [cheering] >> The instinct [music] is older than football. Along highways across the country, drivers pass small shrines wrapped entirely in red. Flags, >> [music] >> ribbons, painted stars. They honor Gauchito Gil, >> [music] >> an outlaw gaucho of the 1800s who robbed the rich, was executed by the law, and was never canonized by any church. Truck drivers sound their horns as they pass. Many stop, leave a cigarette or a coin, and ask for protection on the road. Further west in the desert [music] of San Juan, pilgrims have left a small mountain of water bottles at the shrine of the Difunta Correa. She was a young mother, who died of thirst, the story goes, while her baby survived at her breast. Official religion is one thing here. Argentine faith is bigger, stranger, and always a little outlaw. And every faith needs its weekly service. In Argentina, it falls on Sunday. After church, around a fire. >> The asado is not a barbecue. It is the central institution of Argentine social [music] life, and it runs on protocol. It begins hours before anyone eats, when the asador, the keeper of the fire, starts coaxing hardwood coals toward a temperature that cannot be measured, only known. The role is earned, never assigned. An asador does not leave the grill, does not hurry the meat, and accepts advice from absolutely no one. Around the fire, the rest of the family orbits, setting tables, cutting bread, opening wine, and solving the problems [music] of the nation in conversation. The meal arrives in movements, like a symphony. First, the chorizo sausages and the crisped delicacies for the brave. Then, the ribs. Then, the great cuts, carried to the table on wooden boards through a chorus of approval. And when the meat [music] is right, it is nearly always right, someone raises the oldest toast in the country, "Un aplauso para el asador." A round of applause for the grill master. It is half a joke and entirely sincere. And it may be the only performance review in Argentina that never comes back negative. Outside the stadiums, the asado keeps a fast, loud cousin, the choripan, a grilled sausage [music] split into bread and painted with chimichurri, eaten standing up, dripping in a crowd, ideally minutes before kickoff. And across the country runs the empanada, a folded pastry that every province claims to make best. Salta likes them small and juicy. Tucumán insists the meat must be cut by knife, never minced. Families argue about this the way other families argue about politics, and considerably more fiercely. Dessert, if anyone still has room, means dulce de leche, the slow-cooked milk caramel that Argentines spread on nearly everything and defend as a national invention. When the last board is cleared, nobody moves because after the asado comes the longest sobremesa of the week, stretching into the evening, until somebody finally checks the time and laughs. Someone's uncle has fallen asleep in a chair. Nobody wakes him. This is Argentina on any Sunday in any neighborhood. But beyond the capital, the country plays by even bigger [music] rules. Drive one day in any direction and the world changes completely. Argentina is the eighth largest country on Earth, and it collects climates the way [music] its people collect rituals. Travel northwest and the land climbs into the Andes, >> [music] >> The great gorge of Humahuaca, a trade road older than the Inca Empire, walled in rock striped [music] like a spice market. Adobe villages sit beneath cactus slopes, and in the markets, women sell coca leaves, legal here, chewed or brewed into tea against the brutal [music] altitude. The custom is thousands of years older than any modern border, and a world away from what laboratories make of the same plant. Up here, the Catholic saints share the calendar with Pachamama, Mother Earth, who receives her own offerings before every harvest. >> [music] >> Travel south instead, and the world empties into Patagonia. Glacial lakes glow a turquoise [music] so intense it looks manufactured, and the explanation fits in a single sentence. Ancient ice grinds mountains into a flower so fine, it hangs suspended in the water and scatters the light. Forests hide alerce trees more than 3,000 years old, already seedlings when Rome was young, and ice fields still carve into lakes [music] with a boom that rolls across the water like distant artillery. And in one green river valley in the middle of that emptiness, [music] afternoon tea is served in Welsh. In 1865, a sailing ship called the Mimosa landed around 150 settlers from Wales fleeing to protect their language and faith. They expected green meadows and found a wind-swept desert. They survived by digging some of the first irrigation canals in [music] South America with guidance from the Tehuelche people who already knew the land. >> [music] >> Their descendants still sing in Welsh choirs and run tea houses >> [music] >> in towns called Gaiman and Trevelin. In 1995, Princess Diana herself stopped in Gaiman [music] for tea and Welsh cakes, 10,000 km from Wales and somehow completely at home. Deserts glaciers jungles planes [music] a dozen worlds under one flag, disagreeing cheerfully about [music] nearly everything. All of them agree completely about exactly one thing >> [music] >> once every four years. >> [cheering] >> On the morning of December the 18th, 2022, Argentina went quiet. Shops closed early or never opened. >> [music] >> Highways emptied. In living rooms, bakeries, hospital wards, and fire stations, some 46 million people arranged [music] themselves around screens, wearing unwashed lucky shirts, sitting in their assigned seats, holding their grandmother's hand. In Qatar, the national team was playing France in the final of the World Cup. Argentina had not lifted the trophy [music] in 36 years, a wait that contained an economic collapse, several currencies, and the death of Maradona two years before. The superstitions were all on duty that morning. Shirts unwashed since the opening match, beards a month old, the same seats, the same snacks, the same people [music] arranged like a formula that had worked so far and could not be risked [music] now. For 80 minutes, it looked like a coronation. Two goals ahead, in control, almost [music] serene. Then France scored twice in under two minutes, and a nation's heart stopped [music] in real time. Extra time came. Messi scored again. France answered again. Penalties. [music] There are Argentines who will tell you flatly that they did not breathe [music] during the shootout. And medically speaking, they may not be exaggerating by much. Then, the final penalty went in. And the sound that rose out [music] of Buenos Aires, people swear, could be heard across the river in Uruguay. What happened next had no precedent. Millions poured into the streets [music] within minutes. Strangers embracing, old men weeping on balconies, entire [music] avenues singing with one voice. >> [music] >> Two days later, the government declared [music] a national holiday for the victory parade, and the crowd around the obelisco was estimated by local media at 4 million people, one of the largest gatherings in the country's history. In the crowd, >> [music] >> many held up photographs of parents and grandparents who had not lived to see this day, so [music] that, in a way, they could watch it, too. The gathering grew so dense that the parade had to be abandoned [music] partway. The champions of the world could not physically reach their own celebration. They finished the day waving from helicopters instead, while below them, an entire nation had stopped [music] checking the price of absolutely anything. >> [music] >> So, ask the question this whole journey has been circling. Why does one country need football this much? Not enjoy it, need it. The answer is scattered through everything we have passed. In a place where the currency can betray you, where plans dissolve and governments turn over, the things that hold are the things that repeat. The mate that comes around the circle every morning, the sobremesa after every meal, the ñoquis on every 29th, the asado every Sunday, and the match every weekend in every neighborhood forever. >> Football is simply the largest ritual of them all. The only one big enough to hold the whole country at once. It cannot lose its value overnight. It cannot be devalued, defaulted on, or quietly converted into [music] dollars. Whatever the month has done to your savings, on Sunday, the whistle blows, the neighborhood club opens its doors, the potrero fills with children, and for 90 minutes, Argentina is exactly what it has always been. It is not an escape from real life here. It is the most dependable part of it. It is also why grown adults cry over football here, openly, and why nobody ever mocks them for it. They are not crying about a game. They are crying about every year this same fixture held the family together. The grandfather who chose their club for them, the summers on [music] the terraces, the bad seasons survived side by side. In Argentina, a football club is a family tree you can watch on television. People will tell you their country is [music] a promise that keeps breaking and a party that never quite ends, both at once. And they will tell you this while pouring you another glass. Maybe that is the real answer. Argentina is not a place that avoids heartbreak. It is a place that decided [music] long ago that heartbreak would never get the last word. Not while there is a fire lit, a table full, a ball rolling, and someone beside you waiting for the mate. Remember the empty Sunday streets from the beginning of this journey? Now you know where everyone was. Not hiding from their troubles, attending faithfully the one appointment in the country that has never once defaulted. And when the final [music] whistle blows, they will pour back out onto those streets, win or lose, and set the table again. Because the anchor holds. It always has. So tell us, in your country, what is the anchor? The one thing that stays [music] certain when everything else changes. Write it below. And if you are Argentine, tell us honestly how close we came. We read every single comment. And subscribing keeps journeys like this going.
